title: Standard and custom objects
objectives: Map object, field, and record to the shared shape, typed attribute, and saved occurrence they represent.
Distinguish Salesforce-created standard objects from organization-created custom objects without treating either as a default design choice.
Separate metadata that defines or presents a model from business data stored in records and field values.
Keep a user-facing label, machine-facing API name, and optional custom tab as different boundaries.
Diagnose object existence, actor access, and visible navigation as separate gates with observable evidence.
Choose and defend a synthetic LAB_ object model, then transfer the decision to a changed business context.
diagnostic_question: A facilities team asks to track properties in Salesforce. Before reading the lesson, decide whether the need is an object, record, field, metadata, business data, or navigation; what evidence would make you choose standard versus custom; and what would you check if a user cannot see the result?
definition: An object is the shared definition for a kind of Salesforce data; fields describe attributes and records are saved occurrences. Salesforce's Object Reference uses table, column, and row as a structural analogy, while standard versus custom describes who created the object—not whether it is accessible or visible. ([Object Reference](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_concepts.htm); [Trailhead](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/data_modeling/objects_intro))
why_it_matters: A wrong boundary creates downstream rework: a record may be mistaken for a definition, a tab may be mistaken for an object, or a custom object may be created before the standard model is understood. Separating shape, data, access, and presentation gives an administrator a smaller diagnostic search space and a safer release conversation.
sixty_second_explanation: Think in four gates: define the shared object shape, choose standard or custom by semantic fit, create a record as business data, then verify access and navigation separately. Explicit boundaries: object ≠ tab; object definition ≠ record instance; metadata ≠ business data; label ≠ API name; object existence ≠ user access ≠ visible navigation.
deeper_explanation: The Object Reference and Trailhead map object to table, field to column, and record to row as a starting analogy. The analogy explains structure, not the complete behavior of authorization, automation, transactions, or presentation. ([Object Reference](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_concepts.htm); [Trailhead](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/data_modeling/objects_intro))

Salesforce-created objects are standard objects; objects created by an organization through supported configuration or metadata mechanisms are custom objects. Reuse a standard meaning when it fits; treat the choice to create a custom object as a semantic-fit decision for the requirement, not as a universal platform mandate. ([Object Reference](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_concepts.htm); [Trailhead](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/data_modeling/objects_intro))

Metadata describes the model and configuration, including schema, process, presentation, authorization, and other customization concerns; business data is the record information that the organization operates on. The Metadata API guide distinguishes customization metadata from ordinary record CRUD, so a definition change and a saved occurrence need different evidence. ([Understanding Metadata API](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_intro.htm); [Object Reference](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.object_reference.meta/object_reference/sforce_api_objects_concepts.htm))

For a custom object, the Metadata API reference describes a fully specified CustomObject fullName and the automatic __c suffix. Trailhead separately shows custom-object creation and a Custom Tab Wizard; that separation is why an API name or tab should never be used as proof that a record exists or that a user has access. ([CustomObject](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customobject.htm); [Trailhead](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/data_modeling/objects_intro); [Understanding Metadata API](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_intro.htm))

The handbook decision table is a heuristic, not a Salesforce mandate: first name the business noun and its grain, then test standard semantic fit, then consider a custom model, and finally prove the result with a target-user and synthetic-record check. Security, automation dependencies, relationship grain, scale/operability, reporting or integration contracts, and rollback deserve explicit architecture checks; detailed mechanics and numeric limits remain out of scope. Availability and UI steps remain release-, edition-, license-, package-, configuration-, and permission-sensitive.

mental_model.analogy: Blueprint plus filing cabinet: metadata is the shared blueprint, an object is a drawer type, a field is a typed slot, and a record is one filed occurrence. Access controls are keys; a tab is a sign pointing to a drawer.
useful_mapping: object → shared definition for a kind of data
field → named, typed attribute on that definition
record → one saved occurrence with values
metadata → model, process, presentation, or authorization configuration
business data → saved records and values
label/API name/tab → human wording, machine identifier, optional navigation surface
where_it_breaks: The table analogy stops at authorization: an object's existence does not tell us which actor may open it.
It stops at automation and transactions: a save can be validated, automated, committed, or rolled back.
It stops at presentation: a tab or app navigation entry is not the object definition.
Standard versus custom describes origin and model ownership, not quality, security, or universal availability.
An external object is a distinct boundary: its record data is stored outside the Salesforce org, so do not infer custom-object storage or CRUD behavior from the shared word 'object'.
External, big, and event object mechanics are neighboring topics; detailed field types belong to DATA-002 and relationship mechanics to DATA-003.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: An object is shared shape, a field is a typed attribute, and a record is one saved occurrence. Standard means Salesforce-created and custom means organization-created; I choose by semantic fit, not by habit. I keep metadata, business data, access, and optional tab navigation separate.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I begin with the business noun, grain, lifecycle, and actors. I check whether a standard object already expresses that meaning, then consider a custom object only if the organization-defined concept needs its own model. I distinguish the metadata definition and identifiers from the records and values that users operate on. For a visibility problem, I verify existence, actor permissions and sharing, navigation/presentation, and a known synthetic record independently. I scope every UI, API, edition, package, and limit statement to the target org and test the design in a disposable environment.

terminology.plain: The shared definition for one kind of Salesforce data.
terminology.precise: An object is the model boundary that gives a kind of data a name and shared structure; the table analogy is useful for structure but does not make an object a screen or a record.
terminology.example: Account is a standard object; LAB_Property__c is a synthetic custom-object example for a property model.
terminology.non_example: A Custom Tab or an individual LAB_Property__c row is not the object definition.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Record: one saved occurrence of the object, not the shared definition.
terminology.boundary: This lesson establishes object grain and standard/custom boundaries; detailed fields, types, IDs, and relationships continue in DATA-002 and DATA-003.

terminology.plain: One saved occurrence of an object, with values for its fields.
terminology.precise: A record is an instance of an object that represents one occurrence of the modeled thing; it is business data, not the metadata that defines the object.
terminology.example: A synthetic record LAB-PROP-001 represents one test property with LAB_ values.
terminology.non_example: Saving the LAB_Property__c definition or a Custom Tab does not create a business record.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Field: a named attribute within the model; a record contains field values.
terminology.boundary: Record IDs, detailed data types, and record-operation mechanics are introduced here only enough to separate an occurrence from its definition; see DATA-002.

terminology.plain: A named slot for one typed attribute of a record.
terminology.precise: A field is part of an object's shared structure and supplies an attribute whose value can differ from record to record.
terminology.example: Status__c can hold the synthetic lifecycle value Draft on LAB-PROP-001.
terminology.non_example: The value Draft is not the field definition, and a tab is not a field.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Label: display wording for people; a field is a model attribute with values.
terminology.boundary: This lesson uses fields to explain object grain only; field types, requiredness, and validation belong to DATA-002.

terminology.plain: An object Salesforce created as part of the platform model.
terminology.precise: Standard identifies the object's Salesforce-created origin; it does not promise universal access, a particular tab, or a perfect fit for every requirement.
terminology.example: Account is a familiar standard object whose meaning should be checked before modeling a customer-related need elsewhere.
terminology.non_example: Renaming the Account label to Property does not create a custom object or change the underlying standard object's origin.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Custom object: organization-created data model definition, not a synonym for a lower-quality object.
terminology.boundary: Standard/custom origin is the scope here; availability, licensing, packages, relationships, and object-specific behavior require current target-org checks.

terminology.plain: An object an organization creates for an organization-specific data model.
terminology.precise: A custom object is organization-created metadata for a distinct kind of data; the Metadata API reference describes a fully specified name and the automatic __c suffix.
terminology.example: LAB_Property__c is a synthetic custom-object candidate when the property concept needs its own model after standard-fit discovery.
terminology.non_example: Creating a Custom Tab or renaming a label does not create a custom object.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Custom tab: presentation/navigation metadata that may point to an object but is not the object's data definition.
terminology.boundary: Custom means organization-created, not automatically correct; verify standard fit, scope, access, package behavior, and target-org availability first.

terminology.plain: Shared definitions and configuration that describe how the platform is shaped or behaves.
terminology.precise: The Metadata API guide groups metadata concerns such as schema, processes, presentation, authorization, and configuration; metadata is distinct from ordinary business records.
terminology.example: Defining LAB_Property__c, its label/API name, and an optional CustomTab is metadata work.
terminology.non_example: A saved LAB-PROP-001 record with Status__c = Draft is business data, not the object definition.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Business data: records and values that represent the organization's operating state.
terminology.boundary: Metadata customization and ordinary record CRUD use different evidence paths; do not infer that a metadata deployment inserted records.

terminology.plain: The saved records and values that describe the organization's modeled work.
terminology.precise: Business data is the operational information held in records and field values; it is separate from the metadata that defines the container and its presentation.
terminology.example: LAB-PROP-001 with a synthetic address label and Draft status is business data in the lab.
terminology.non_example: The API name LAB_Property__c or a CustomTab definition is not a business-data record.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Metadata: the shared model/configuration that makes the record shape possible.
terminology.boundary: Use a separate record/data-operation check for business data; do not claim that a successful customization change proves data presence.

terminology.plain: The human-facing name users read for an object or feature.
terminology.precise: A label is display wording chosen for people; it is different from the machine-facing API name used to identify a model in tools and integrations.
terminology.example: LAB Property is the readable label for the synthetic LAB_Property__c object.
terminology.non_example: LAB_Property__c is an API name, not the user-facing label; a tab icon is not a label.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: API name: machine identifier; changing or reading one does not establish the other's role.
terminology.boundary: Trailhead's creation flow treats label and Object Name as distinct inputs; reverify exact labels and UI behavior in the target release/org.

terminology.plain: The machine-facing identifier used to refer to a model in tools and integrations.
terminology.precise: An API name is the identifier that distinguishes a model for programmatic or metadata operations; custom-object names conventionally receive the __c suffix described by the CustomObject reference.
terminology.example: LAB_Property__c is the synthetic custom-object API name paired with the label LAB Property.
terminology.non_example: LAB Property is readable label text, not the API name; a user's permission is not an API name.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Label: human wording that should not be substituted for machine identity.
terminology.boundary: API syntax, namespaces, package behavior, and availability are release- and target-org-sensitive; the __c suffix does not grant access or create navigation.

terminology.plain: An optional presentation and navigation surface for users.
terminology.precise: A CustomTab is presentation metadata that can help expose an object in navigation; it is not the object definition, a record, or an access grant.
terminology.example: A LAB Property custom tab may be added after the object model and target-user access are verified.
terminology.non_example: Creating a tab alone does not create LAB_Property__c or a LAB-PROP-001 record.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Object: the shared data definition that a tab may help users reach.
terminology.boundary: Navigation is one observation gate; check object access, field/record visibility, app assignment, and known-record evidence separately.

terminology.plain: An object-shaped Salesforce surface whose records remain in an outside system.
terminology.precise: An external object maps to data stored outside the Salesforce organization; it is a distinct object kind from an org-stored custom object, even though both can be discussed as objects.
terminology.example: A target-org-approved external object that reads synthetic ERP test data without copying the source records into Salesforce.
terminology.non_example: LAB_Property__c is an org-defined custom-object candidate; pointing an integration at it does not make its records external.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Custom object: an organization-created model whose records are stored in the Salesforce data model.
terminology.boundary: The source documents the storage boundary and __x naming convention; connector, callout, license, security, performance, and availability details require separate target-org verification.

terminology.plain: The org or package context used to resolve a machine-facing metadata identity.
terminology.precise: CustomObject metadata requires a fully specified fullName; in a namespaced or packaged context, read the target metadata identity as delivered rather than stripping or inventing a prefix.
terminology.example: Before writing a query or deployment manifest, compare the target org's fully specified object name with the package or local model context.
terminology.non_example: Assuming every object ending in __c has the same unqualified identity in every org or package.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Custom-object suffix: __c identifies the custom-object naming convention; namespace/package context is a separate identity boundary.
terminology.boundary: This lesson does not assert package installation, namespace availability, or a universal prefix syntax; verify the target org, package, and API version.
